881.quote_or_event: When Guru Ram Das installed his youngest son Arjan as the fifth Guru in 1581, his eldest son Prithi Chand resented being passed over, and the succession caused lasting discord among the brothers.
881.explanation: The Guru's own household, which should have been his chief support, became a source of rivalry and grief, and Prithi Chand's opposition dogged Guru Arjan's early years.
881.tie_back: As the Kural says that shade and water turn harmful when they breed sickness, the closeness of kin became painful here precisely because the hostility came from within the family.
881.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Why was Guru Arjan's installation as Guru disputed?' (Britannica Editors)
881._accuracy_note: Strong historical fit for harm arising from one's own kin; the paraphrase keeps to what Britannica states, and the fuller Sikh accounts of Prithi Chand's later hostility were not separately verified this session.

882.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
882.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts a gleaming outward surface with the darkness it hides; in the Janamsakhi tradition this shabad is linked to his meeting with Sajjan, a host who welcomed travellers with a show of piety and then robbed them.
882.tie_back: The Kural warns that the foe who looks like a friend is more to be feared than an open enemy, and Guru Nanak likewise exposes the friendly surface that hides harm.
882.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
882._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on false outward friendliness; the scripture line is verified, but the Sajjan setting comes from Janamsakhi hagiography rather than the text itself.

883.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism.”
883.explanation: Guru Amar Das locates the most dangerous enemies inside the person, as thieves already living within the house of the body who plunder its true wealth.
883.tie_back: The Kural urges guarding oneself against the enemy within before it strikes at a moment of weakness, and Gurbani names that inner enemy as the five thieves.
883.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
883._accuracy_note: Strong on the idea of an enemy within, but Gurbani moves the theme from hidden human foes to inner vices, so the parallel is partly a reinterpretation.

884.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
884.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the mind reformed in the company of the holy, from which enmity has gone so that no one, kin or stranger, seems hostile.
884.tie_back: Where the Kural says hidden enmity in an unreformed mind turns one's own people against one, Gurbani shows the reformed mind in which that enmity cannot take root.
884.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
884._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it gives the positive remedy (a mind free of enmity) rather than the Kural's warning about what an unreformed mind brings.

885.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
885.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses anger directly as the root of strife and a force that leaves no room for compassion.
885.tie_back: The Kural says enmity springing up among kin brings deadly evils, and Gurbani traces such conflict back to anger, which shuts out the compassion that holds a family together.
885.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
885._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on anger as the source of strife; the verse is general and does not speak specifically of kinship or of deadly consequences.

886.quote_or_event: After Maharaja Ranjit Singh died in 1839, the Sikh state he had built broke down within six years through palace revolutions and assassinations, and after two wars with the British the Punjab was annexed in 1849.
886.explanation: A kingdom that had been a formidable power under one ruler fell quickly once its own leaders turned against each other.
886.tie_back: This bears out the Kural's warning that once discord takes hold among those who were united, escaping destruction becomes very hard.
886._accuracy_note: Strong historical illustration of internal discord leading to ruin; it is political history of the Sikh state rather than Sikh religious teaching, and outside causes also played a part.

887.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
887.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, condemns those whose words and inner feelings do not match.
887.tie_back: Like the casket whose lid sits flush yet remains a separate piece, people whose hearts and mouths differ may seem united while being divided inside, as the Kural says.
887.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
887._accuracy_note: Good fit on outward agreement hiding inner division; Farid speaks of a gap between one person's heart and speech, not of a divided family.

888.quote_or_event: “The five thieves plunder their homes, and egotism breaks in.”
888.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the home of the heart being robbed from the inside by the vices, with ego breaking through its walls.
888.tie_back: The Kural pictures a family worn away by enmity within, like metal under a file, and Gurbani likewise shows a house emptied from within rather than by an outside attacker.
888.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 854, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
888._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shares the image of a home ruined from within, but the plunder is by inner vices and is sudden, not the slow wearing-down of a family by feuding.

889.quote_or_event: “Even if the poisonous snake is fed large amounts of milk, it will still yield only poison.”
889.explanation: Guru Ram Das observes that a poisonous nature stays poisonous however much it is nourished, so that the harm remains hidden within.
889.tie_back: The Kural holds that even enmity as small as half a sesame seed contains ruin, and Gurbani likewise says that poison held inside is never made harmless.
889.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 171, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
889._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the idea that latent harm within stays dangerous, but it is about a fixed bad nature, not the small size of a grudge.

890.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them.”
890.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, warns against close company with those cut off from God, whose influence is harmful.
890.tie_back: The Kural compares living with people who do not truly agree with you to sharing a hut with a snake, and Kabir's counsel is to keep away from such company.
890.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Kabeer, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
890._accuracy_note: Partial: the advice to avoid harmful company fits, but Kabir's saakat is someone spiritually faithless rather than a housemate secretly at odds with you, and the snake image is absent.
